4C(s) + 4H2(g) + O2(g) → C3H7COOH(l)

Why: a formation equation makes exactly 1 mol of product from its elements in their standard states, so state symbols are required.

ΔHc = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)

−2183.5 = [4(−393.5) + 4(−285.9)] − [ΔHf(acid) + 5(0)]
−2183.5 = −2717.6 − ΔHf(acid)

ΔHf(butanoic acid) = −534.1 kJ mol−1

Remember ΔHf of an element (O2) is zero.

(i) ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = 2E(A–A) + E(B–B) − 4E(A–B)
Each A2B contains two A–B bonds, so 2A2B has four.

(ii) Tabulated bond enthalpies are average values from many compounds, so they differ from the actual values in the specific molecules (and apply only to gases). Agreement is best for gas-phase reactions in which few bonds are broken, or when specific bond energies are used.

(i) ΔHf° = standard enthalpy change of formation: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. S° = standard (absolute) entropy: a measure of the disorder (dispersal of energy/particles) of one mole of substance in its standard state. The symbol ° means standard conditions: 298 K and 1 atm (100 kPa). Both needed.

(ii) Entropy has absolute values (S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K), so S itself is quoted rather than a change, Δ.

(iii) ΔHf°(Cu) = 0 — an element in its standard state.

(i) The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

(ii) 3C(s) + 4H2(g) → C3H8(g). Exactly one mole of product; state symbols required.

(i) Average bond enthalpy: the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in the gaseous state, averaged over a range of compounds.

Bonds broken: 2(C—C) + 8(C—H) + 5(O=O) = 2(348) + 8(412) + 5(496) = 6472 kJ

Bonds formed: 6(C=O) + 8(O—H) = 6(743) + 8(463) = 8162 kJ

ΔH = 6472 − 8162 = −1690 kJ mol⁻¹ (values from the data booklet used at the time).

(ii) Positive: 6 mol of gas (1 C3H8 + 5 O2) become 7 mol of gas (3 CO2 + 4 H2O(g)), so disorder increases.

(i) Mr(C5H11OH) = 88. Each extra CH2 adds about −650 to −660 kJ mol⁻¹ (a straight line on the graph), so extending the line to Mr = 88 gives ΔHc ≈ −3325 kJ mol⁻¹ (±25). The minus sign is required.

(ii) About the same: pentan-2-ol is a structural isomer, so the same number and types of bonds are broken and formed on combustion. Saying only 'same Mr/formula' does not score.

• Formation: Na(s) + ½Cl2(g) → NaCl(s)
  • Atomization Na: Na(s) → Na(g)
  • Atomization Cl: ½Cl2(g) → Cl(g)
  • 1st IE: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
  • 1st EA: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)

State symbols required. Common errors: Cl2 → 2Cl for atomization (must be per mole of Cl atoms) and Na(s) in the ionization step.

(i) Lattice enthalpy: the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is separated into its gaseous ions (ΔH positive).

(ii) Born–Haber cycle: Na(s) + ½Cl2(g) → (+109) Na(g) → (+121) Na(g) + Cl(g) → (+494) Na⁺(g) + Cl(g) + e⁻ → (−364) Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g); the lattice step links this to NaCl(s); ΔHf = −411.

ΔHf = ΔHat(Na) + ΔHat(Cl) + IE + EA − LE

−411 = 109 + 121 + 494 − 364 − LE → LE = +771 kJ mol⁻¹

Build a cycle to the gaseous atoms. C(g) + 4F(g) → CF4(g):
ΔH = −ΔHat(C) − 2E(F–F) + ΔHf(CF4) = −715 − 2(158) + (−680) = −1711 kJ

This forms 4 C–F bonds, so average C–F bond enthalpy = 1711 ÷ 4 = 428 kJ mol−1 (quoted as positive; bond breaking is endothermic).

Common error: forgetting that 2 mol F2 must be broken to give 4F(g).

Standard enthalpy of formation: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K) [3].

2C(s) + 3H2(g) + ½O2(g) → C2H5OH(l) — [1] formulas/coefficients, [1] state symbols.

Bond enthalpy: energy required to break one mole of a given bond (in gaseous molecules) [1]. Average: the value is the mean for that bond over a range of different compounds, since its strength varies slightly with its environment [1].

Cyclohexane has only C–C and C–H single bonds of normal length/strength, so average bond enthalpies describe it well [2].

Benzene has a delocalised (resonance) π system: all C–C bonds are identical, intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5) [1]. Average C–C/C=C values (Kekulé structure) don't fit, and they ignore the extra stability from delocalisation, so the bond-enthalpy result differs more from the enthalpy-of-formation result [1].

Not standard (ΔH°): the value is at 500 K, not under standard conditions (298 K) [1].

Not formation (ΔHf): this is a decomposition, not the formation of 1 mol of a compound from its elements [1].

ΔHc = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)

−3050 = [6(−394) + 3(−286)] − ΔHf(phenol) = −3222 − ΔHf(phenol)

ΔHf(phenol) = −3222 + 3050 = −172 kJ mol−1

ΔHf(O2) = 0 (element). A sign error (+172) scores max [2].

Standard enthalpy change of formation: the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

½H2(g) + ½N2(g) + 1½O2(g) → HNO3(l)

Writing 2HNO3 or omitting state symbols loses marks.

ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)

= [3(−394) + 2(−286)] − [+185 + 0] = −1754 − 185

= −1939 kJ (ΔHf of propyne, +185 kJ mol−1, from the Data Booklet; O2 = 0).

Using −185 for propyne gives −1569 (scores [3]).

Levels, from bottom up:

  • LiF(s) (lowest)
  • Li(s) + ½F2(g) – linked to LiF(s) by ΔHf
  • Li(g) + ½F2(g) – atomization of Li
  • Li+(g) + e− + ½F2(g) – first IE of Li
  • Li+(g) + e− + F(g) – atomization of F (½ bond enthalpy)
  • Li+(g) + F−(g) – electron affinity of F (downward)

Lattice enthalpy links Li+(g) + F−(g) and LiF(s). Endothermic steps may be in any order; −1 per level with wrong species/state symbols; electrons must be shown.

AgF: experimental (Born–Haber) and theoretical (ionic-model) lattice enthalpies agree closely → bonding essentially ionic.

AgI: experimental value is noticeably larger than the theoretical one → bonding has significant covalent character (the large I− ion is polarized by Ag+).

(i) ΔH°c = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants) = [6(−394) + 6(−242)] − (−43) = −3816 + 43 = −3773 kJ mol−1 (≈ −3.8 × 103). +3773 scores [1].

(ii) ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants) = [6(214) + 6(189)] − [385 + 9(205)] = 2418 − 2230 = +188 J K−1 mol−1. −188 scores [1].

Why positive: 10 mol gas → 12 mol gas (water is vapour here).

Use: reverse equation 1 (+676) + equation 2 (−394) + 2 × equation 3 (2 × −242 = −484).

ΔH4 = +676 − 394 − 484 = −202 kJ mol−1

Common errors: not reversing ΔH1 or not doubling ΔH3 (+202 or +40 score [3]).
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa). Do not say “heat needed” and do not omit “1 mol”.
ΔHf⦵ of H2O(l) is more negative (greater in magnitude) than that of H2O(g), because extra energy is released when steam condenses to liquid water.

ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)
= [(−28) + (−242)] − [(−201) + (−46)]
= −270 − (−247) = −23 kJ mol−1.

Sign and units are needed for full marks. Using −239 (liquid methanol) instead of −201 (gas) is a common slip.
The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

(i) ΣΔHf(products) = 4(−394) + 4(−242) = −2544 kJ. ΣΔHf(reactants) = +1 kJ (O2 = 0).
ΔH = −2544 − (+1) = −2545 kJ mol−1.

(ii) The products are more stable. The reaction is exothermic, so the products have lower enthalpy (stronger bonds) than the reactants.

(iii) It would be the same. Both isomers have the same bonds (1 C=C, 2 C–C, 8 C–H) and give the same products, so average bond enthalpies give the same value.

(i) The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance is formed from its elements in their standard states, under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

(ii) Cycle: the elements 2C(s) + 3H2(g) + 3½O2(g) go either directly to 2CO2 + 3H2O, or first to C2H5OH(l) + 3O2 and then by combustion.
ΔHf(C2H5OH) + ΔHc = 2ΔHf(CO2) + 3ΔHf(H2O)
ΔHf = 2(−394) + 3(−286) − (−1371) = −275 kJ mol−1.
Without a drawn cycle the maximum is [3].

(i) The energy needed to break 1 mol of a given bond with all species in the gaseous state, averaged over a range of similar compounds.

(ii) The two C–H bonds of ethyne are unchanged. Broken: C≡C + 2 H–H = 837 + 2(436) = 1709 kJ. Formed: C–C + 4 C–H = 348 + 4(412) = 1996 kJ.
ΔH = 1709 − 1996 = −287 kJ mol−1.

(iii) Bond enthalpy decreases C–Cl > C–Br > C–I. The halogen atom is larger down the group, so the bond is longer and the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus.

(i) Cyclohexatriene would have three isolated C=C bonds: 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol−1.

(ii) Less heat is released (−207 kJ mol−1) because benzene is about 153 kJ mol−1 more stable than cyclohexatriene, due to delocalization of its π electrons. It does not contain three separate C=C bonds.

The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

C(s) + 2H2(g) + ½O2(g) → CH3OH(l)

The balanced equation earns 1 mark and the state symbols 1 mark. You must form 1 mol of product, so write ½O2.

Average bond enthalpy: the energy needed to break 1 mol of a bond in the gaseous state, averaged over a range of similar compounds.

Broken: 2 C=O + 3 H–H = 2(743) + 3(436) = 2794 kJ

Formed: 3 C–H + C–O + 3 O–H (one O–H in CH3OH, two in H2O) = 3(412) + 360 + 3(463) = 2985 kJ

ΔH = 2794 − 2985 = −191 kJ

ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = −487 − [(−239) + (−111)] = −137 kJ

Use the value for liquid methanol.

(i) Average bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a given bond, with all species in the gaseous state, averaged over the values for that bond in a range of similar compounds.

(ii) The H–H bond occurs only in the H2 molecule. Its bond enthalpy is an exact value for that one molecule, so there is nothing to average over.

Hess's law: burn the elements, then reverse the combustion of octane.

  • 8C: 8 × (−394) = −3152 kJ
  • 9H2: 9 × (−286) = −2574 kJ
  • Reverse octane combustion: +5512 kJ

ΔHf = −3152 − 2574 + 5512 = −214 kJ mol−1

Equivalently, ΔHf = ΣΔHc(reactants) − ΣΔHc(products).

• Atomization (sublimation) of K: K(s) → K(g)
  • First ionization energy of K: K(g) → K+(g) + e−
  • Atomization of fluorine (½ the F–F bond enthalpy): ½F2(g) → F(g)
  • Electron affinity of F: F(g) + e− → F−(g)

Each mark needs both the name and the equation with correct state symbols.

• If benzene had three separate C=C bonds, its hydrogenation would release 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ.
  • Only −208 kJ is released, so real benzene is about 152 kJ more stable than the Kekulé structure.
  • The circle in the hexagon represents this delocalized π system (a resonance hybrid), not alternating single and double bonds.

(i) A: enthalpy of atomization (sublimation) of Mg. B: atomization of oxygen (½ × O=O bond enthalpy). D: sum of first and second electron affinities of oxygen (O → O− → O2−). "Vaporization" not accepted for A or B.

(ii) F is the standard enthalpy change of formation of MgO: the enthalpy change when 1 mol of the compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, under standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).

(iii) F = A + B + C + D + E: −602 = 150 + 248 + 2186 + 702 + E, so E = −3888 kJ mol−1 (3888 also accepted; quoting the data-booklet 3889 is not).

(iv) First ionization energy: the energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms (Mg(g) → Mg+(g) + e⁻). The second value is larger because the electron is removed from a positive ion: less electron–electron repulsion / greater effective nuclear attraction on the remaining electrons.

(v) MgO: its ions carry double charges (2+ and 2−) versus 1+ and 1− in NaF, so at a similar inter-ionic distance the electrostatic attraction is much greater.

(i) Target: C2H6 → C2H4 + H2.
½ eqn 1: C2H6 + 3½O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O, ΔH = −1560
reverse ½ eqn 2: H2O → H2 + ½O2, ΔH = +286
reverse eqn 3: 2CO2 + 2H2O → C2H4 + 3O2, ΔH = +1411
Sum: ΔH° = +137 kJ (−137 scores [2]).

(ii) ΔS° positive: the number of moles of gas increases (1 → 2).

(iii) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. At low T, ΔH dominates so ΔG is positive (non-spontaneous); at high T the −TΔS term dominates so ΔG becomes negative (spontaneous).

(iv) Bonds broken: C–C + 6 C–H = 347 + 6(413) = 2825 kJ. Bonds formed: C=C + H–H + 4 C–H = 612 + 436 + 4(413) = 2700 kJ. ΔH = 2825 − 2700 = +125 kJ (−125 not accepted).

(v) Bond enthalpies are average values from many compounds, so they are not exact for these specific molecules.

(i) I = enthalpy of atomization (sublimation) of magnesium, Mg(s) → Mg(g). V = standard enthalpy of formation of MgCl2(s).

(ii) II = atomization of Cl2 = +243 kJ; III = 738 + 1451 = +2189 kJ; IV = 2 × (−349) = −698 kJ. Going round the cycle: ΔHlat = −V + I + II + III + IV = 642 + 148 + 243 + 2189 − 698 = +2524 kJ mol−1. A common error is using −349 only once.

(iii) The theoretical value assumes a purely ionic model. The experimental value is larger because MgCl2 has some covalent character: the small Mg2+ polarizes Cl−.

(iv) O2− has a greater charge and a smaller radius than Cl−, so the attraction to Mg2+ is stronger.

(i) ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = 2(−286) − (+50.6) = −622.6 kJ mol−1. ΔHf is zero for N2 and O2.

(ii) Bonds broken: 4(N–H) + N–N + O=O = 4(391) + 158 + 498 = 2220 kJ. Bonds formed: N≡N + 4(O–H) = 945 + 4(464) = 2801 kJ. ΔH = 2220 − 2801 = −581 kJ mol−1.

(iii) The ΔHf value is more accurate. ΔHf data are specific to the actual compounds, whereas bond enthalpies are averages that apply only to gases (they ignore intermolecular forces in the liquids).

(iv) ΔS = [191 + 2(69.9)] − [205 + 121] = +4.8 J K−1 mol−1. It is small because there is the same number of moles of gas on each side (1 → 1).

(v) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −622.6 − 298(0.0048) = −624.0 kJ mol−1.

(vi) It is spontaneous at all temperatures: ΔH is negative and ΔS is positive, so ΔG is always negative.
